note: Front lines, occupied areas and arrows are approximate reconstructions traced by hand from campaign maps (chiefly the US Military Academy atlas of the Great War) and clipped to 1914 borders; they show the general shape and timing of each front, not exact trench positions.

chapters.title: The sweep through Belgium
arrows: German advance through Belgium and France (Schlieffen Plan)
chapters.text: Germany planned to defeat France in about six weeks by swinging through neutral Belgium. Its armies crossed the border on 4 August, which brought Britain into the war, took Liège and Brussels and pushed the French and British back towards Paris, while French offensives into Lorraine and the Ardennes were thrown back.

chapters.title: Tannenberg and Galicia
arrows: Russian First Army invades East Prussia
Russian Second Army advances into southern East Prussia
Tannenberg: German Eighth Army encircles the Russian Second Army
German counter-attack at the Masurian Lakes
chapters.text: Russia attacked sooner than Germany expected, invading East Prussia from the east and the south. The Germans encircled and destroyed the southern army at Tannenberg (26–30 August) and drove the other out at the Masurian Lakes (7–14 September). Further south, Austria-Hungary's push into Russian Poland stalled, while the Russians overran eastern Galicia, took Lemberg on 3 September and drove the Austrians back towards the Carpathians.

chapters.title: Stopped on the Marne
arrows: Race to the Sea: German outflanking moves
chapters.text: French and British counter-attacks on the Marne (5–12 September) forced the Germans back to the Aisne. Each side then tried to get round the other's northern flank in the 'Race to the Sea'; Antwerp fell on 10 October and the Allies held Ypres through a month of fighting. By December a line of trenches ran from the Belgian coast to Switzerland.

chapters.title: Gallipoli
arrows: Suvla Bay landing and August offensive
chapters.text: To open the straits to Russia and knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war, British, French, Australian and New Zealand troops landed at Cape Helles and Anzac Cove on 25 April 1915. Ottoman defenders held them to beachheads a few kilometres deep; a fresh landing at Suvla Bay and the August attack on the Sari Bair ridge failed too. Anzac and Suvla were evacuated on 20 December 1915 and Helles by 9 January 1916.

chapters.title: The Great Retreat
arrows: Central Powers summer offensive and the Russian Great Retreat
German advance on Kovno and Vilna
chapters.text: A German and Austro-Hungarian attack at Gorlice broke the Russian line on 2 May 1915; Przemyśl was retaken on 3 June and Lemberg on 22 June. Over the summer Russia gave up Poland, Lithuania and most of Courland: Warsaw fell on 5 August, Brest-Litovsk on 26 August and Vilna in mid-September, and the front moved hundreds of kilometres east.

chapters.title: Serbia overrun
arrows: Bulgarian First Army drive on Niš
Allied advance up the Vardar from Salonika
chapters.text: On 6 October 1915 German and Austro-Hungarian armies crossed the Sava and Danube and took Belgrade on 9 October; from 14 October Bulgaria attacked from the east, cutting the railway to Salonika. A French and British force landed at Salonika and pushed up the Vardar, but was driven back into Greece by 12 December. Cornered in Kosovo, the Serbian army retreated over the Montenegrin and Albanian mountains to the Adriatic; the survivors were shipped to Corfu and later fought on the Salonika front.

chapters.title: Verdun and the Somme
chapters.text: Germany attacked Verdun in February 1916 to wear down the French army. To relieve it, Britain and France attacked on the Somme on 1 July; the British suffered about 57,000 casualties on the first day alone. Both battles cost hundreds of thousands of lives for a few kilometres of ground, and by December the French had retaken Fort Douaumont and most of the ground lost at Verdun.

chapters.title: Brusilov and Romania
arrows: Falkenhayn breaks through the Carpathians to Bucharest
chapters.text: General Brusilov's offensive, launched on 4 June 1916, broke the Austro-Hungarian front and took Lutsk and Czernowitz, Russia's greatest success of the war. Encouraged, Romania joined the Allies in August and invaded Transylvania, but German, Austro-Hungarian and Bulgarian armies struck back and took Bucharest on 6 December.

chapters.title: Caporetto
chapters.text: After eleven costly battles on the Isonzo, Austro-German forces broke through at Caporetto on 24 October 1917 and took Udine on the 28th. The Italian army fell back to the Tagliamento and then more than 100 km to the Piave river and Monte Grappa, where it held from about 10 November; British and French divisions arrived to reinforce it.

chapters.title: Jerusalem
arrows: Allenby takes Beersheba, Gaza and Jerusalem
XXI Corps takes Gaza and advances to Jaffa
chapters.text: In Palestine, General Allenby's British Empire forces broke the Ottoman line at Beersheba and Gaza and entered Jerusalem on 11 December 1917.

chapters.title: Russia leaves the war
arrows: Operation Faustschlag: advance on Dvinsk, Pskov and Narva
German advance to Kharkov and Rostov
chapters.text: After the Bolshevik revolution Russia asked for peace. When talks stalled, German armies advanced almost unopposed in February 1918, and on 3 March Russia signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, giving up Poland, the Baltic lands and Ukraine. German and Austro-Hungarian troops went on to occupy Ukraine, reaching Kharkov in April and Rostov in May.

chapters.title: Germany's last gamble
arrows: German spring offensive: Aisne drive to the Marne
chapters.text: With troops freed from the east, Germany attacked in the West on 21 March 1918, before American armies could arrive in strength. Its offensives drove deep bulges towards Amiens, across the Lys and down to the Marne by early June, but cost Germany its best troops. A last push over the Marne on 15 July failed, and from 18 July French and American counter-attacks drove the Germans back to the Vesle.

chapters.title: The other fronts collapse
arrows: Allied breakthrough on the Salonika front (Vardar offensive)
Battle of Megiddo and pursuit to Damascus
chapters.text: In autumn 1918 the Allies broke through in Macedonia, and Bulgaria signed an armistice on 29 September. Victory at Megiddo in Palestine was followed by the Ottoman armistice on 30 October, and Vittorio Veneto in Italy by Austria-Hungary's on 3 November.

chapters.title: The Hundred Days and the armistice
chapters.text: From Amiens on 8 August the Allies, now joined by large American armies, pushed the Germans back in a rolling series of offensives. With its allies gone and revolution at home, Germany signed an armistice that took effect at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918.
